title: Bagging vs Boosting
abstract:
The two ensemble families side by side. They look similar — both combine many
models of the same kind — but they are opposites in almost every respect: what
base learner they want, how they train, how they weight the members, which error
term they attack, and how they behave under noise. This document sets out every
difference, explains why each follows from the bias–variance decomposition, and
gives the decision rule for choosing between them.

blocks.t: The Recap
From the notes

We need LBLV models. Regularization, bagging and boosting are the 3
techniques (Topic 40).

Bagging and boosting both build one low-bias, low-variance model out of many
imperfect ones — but they start from opposite corners of the bias–variance
plane and move in opposite directions.
The Comparison
From the notes

head: BAGGING
BOOSTING
rows: Uses LBHV models — e.g. a fully grown decision tree
Uses HBLV models — e.g. a shallow D.T, max_depth$=1$

[4pt]
Does parallel learning — all models are trained at the same time
Does sequential learning — step by step, one model after another

[4pt]
Weightage of base learners is the same — each model has an equal say

Weightage of base learners is different — a better model has a better
 say, and vice versa

blocks.cap:
The structural difference. Bagging fans out — every model is
 independent and sees a different sample. Boosting is a chain — each model is
 fitted to what the previous one got wrong.

blocks.t: Why Each Property Follows From the Other
Everything follows from which error term you attack

Recall from Topic 40 that averaging reduces variance and leaves bias
untouched, while sequential correction reduces bias. Every other difference
is a consequence:

head: Because\ldots
Bagging
Boosting
rows: \ldots it therefore needs base models that are
LBHV — deep trees, plenty of variance to remove
HBLV — stumps, plenty of bias to remove
\ldots and the members can be trained
In parallel — they need nothing from each other
Able to overfit — more stages means more bias removed, then noise fitted

blocks.cap:
Left: the decomposition, measured. Bagging collapses the variance of a
 deep tree; boosting collapses the bias of a stump. Middle: fit times — bagging
 parallelises, boosting cannot. Right: behaviour under label noise.

head: Bagging
Boosting
rows: High — rate, depth and count interact

blocks.t: Boosting can overfit; bagging essentially cannot

Adding trees to a bag drives $\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$ to zero and nothing else
changes — so $B$ is safe to maximise. Adding stages to a boosted model keeps
reducing training error, and past a point that means fitting noise. This
is why boosting needs n_estimators tuned with early stopping while a
forest does not.
Choosing

head: Use bagging / random forest when
Use boosting when
rows: Labels are noisy or the data is messy
The data is clean and well-labelled
You want a strong result with almost no tuning
Training time matters and you have cores
You want the last few points of accuracy
You need the best tabular benchmark score

blocks.t: The honest practical answer

On clean tabular data a well-tuned gradient-boosting model (Topics 67–69) is
usually the most accurate thing available, and it wins most competitions. A random
forest is the better default: it is far harder to misconfigure, degrades
gracefully under noise, parallelises, and gives an OOB estimate for free. Fit a
forest first to establish what is achievable, then try boosting if the extra
accuracy is worth the tuning effort.
Code

import numpy as np, time
from sklearn.ensemble import (BaggingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier,
                              AdaBoostClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier)
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 12))
y = (1.5*X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - .8*X[:, 2] + .6*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. EACH WANTS THE OPPOSITE BASE LEARNER
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'base learner':22s} {'alone':>8s} {'BAGGED':>9s} {'BOOSTED':>9s}")
for tag, depth in [("stump      (HBLV)", 1),
                   ("depth 3", 3),
                   ("deep tree  (LBHV)", None)]:
    alone = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0),
                            X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    bag = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth),
                                            n_estimators=150, random_state=0),
                          X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    boo = cross_val_score(AdaBoostClassifier(
              DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth or 8),
              n_estimators=150, random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{tag:22s} {alone:8.4f} {bag:9.4f} {boo:9.4f}")
# Bagging gains most from the DEEP tree (variance to remove).
# Boosting gains most from the STUMP (bias to remove).

# =====================================================================
# 2. EQUAL vs UNEQUAL WEIGHTS
# =====================================================================
bag = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=50,
                        random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
ada = AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=50, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\nbagging: every model's weight is 1/{len(bag.estimators_)} = "
      f"{1/len(bag.estimators_):.4f} -- EQUAL SAY")
print(f"boosting alpha weights: min {ada.estimator_weights_.min():.4f}  "
      f"max {ada.estimator_weights_.max():.4f}  "
      f"ratio {ada.estimator_weights_.max()/ada.estimator_weights_.min():.1f}x")
print(f"first five alphas: {ada.estimator_weights_[:5].round(4)}")
# A better model gets a better say -- exactly as the notes state.

# =====================================================================
# 3. PARALLEL vs SEQUENTIAL
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'model':30s} {'fit time':>10s}")
for tag, m in [("bagging  n_jobs=1",  BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                        n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=1)),
               ("bagging  n_jobs=-1", BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                        n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)),
               ("AdaBoost (no n_jobs)", AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=300,
                                                           random_state=0)),
               ("GradientBoosting",   GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=300,
                                                                 random_state=0))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{tag:30s} {time.perf_counter()-t0:9.2f}s")
print("\nboosting has no n_jobs for the boosting loop: stage m+1 needs stage m")

# =====================================================================
# 4. MORE MEMBERS -- always safe vs able to overfit
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'n_estimators':>13s} {'RF train':>10s} {'RF test':>9s} "
      f"{'GB train':>10s} {'GB test':>9s}")
for B in [10, 50, 200, 800, 3000]:
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=B, random_state=0,
                                n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=B, learning_rate=0.3,
                                    max_depth=4, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{B:13d} {rf.score(X_tr,y_tr):10.4f} {rf.score(X_te,y_te):9.4f} "
          f"{gb.score(X_tr,y_tr):10.4f} {gb.score(X_te,y_te):9.4f}")
# The forest's test score plateaus and stays. The boosted model's training
# score marches to 1.000 and its test score eventually turns down.

# =====================================================================
# 5. NOISE ROBUSTNESS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'% flipped':>10s} {'RandomForest':>14s} {'AdaBoost':>10s} "
      f"{'GradBoost':>11s}")
for f in [0.0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30]:
    yn = y_tr.copy()
    fl = rng.random(len(yn)) < f
    yn[fl] = 1 - yn[fl]
    r = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0,
                               n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, yn).score(X_te, y_te)
    a = AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, yn).score(X_te, y_te)
    g = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200,
                                   random_state=0).fit(X_tr, yn).score(X_te, y_te)
    print(f"{f:10.0%} {r:14.4f} {a:10.4f} {g:11.4f}")
# Bagging averages the noise away. AdaBoost's exponential loss chases it.
# Gradient boosting with log loss sits in between.

# =====================================================================
# 6. TUNING BURDEN
# =====================================================================
print("\nout-of-the-box, with NO tuning at all:")
for tag, m in [("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)),
               ("AdaBoost",     AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=0)),
               ("GradientBoost", GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))]:
    print(f"  {tag:16s} {cross_val_score(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean():.4f}")

print("\ngradient boosting is sensitive to its settings:")
for lr, d, ne in [(1.0, 8, 500), (0.3, 4, 300), (0.05, 3, 500), (0.01, 3, 100)]:
    s = cross_val_score(GradientBoostingClassifier(learning_rate=lr, max_depth=d,
                                                   n_estimators=ne, random_state=0),
                        X_tr, y_tr, cv=4).mean()
    print(f"  lr={lr:<5} depth={d} n={ne:<4} -> {s:.4f}")
print("\nthe forest's settings barely matter:")
for mf, d in [("sqrt", None), (None, None), ("sqrt", 6), ("log2", 20)]:
    s = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(max_features=mf, max_depth=d,
                                               n_estimators=200, random_state=0,
                                               n_jobs=-1), X_tr, y_tr, cv=4, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"  max_features={str(mf):<5} depth={str(d):<5} -> {s:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint

rf_default = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0,
                                    n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
gb_tuned = RandomizedSearchCV(
    GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
    {"n_estimators": randint(100, 600), "learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.3),
     "max_depth": randint(2, 6), "subsample": [0.7, 0.85, 1.0]},
    n_iter=20, cv=4, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\nrandom forest, defaults      : {rf_default.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"gradient boosting, 20 trials : {gb_tuned.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"gain from tuning boosting    : "
      f"{gb_tuned.score(X_te, y_te) - rf_default.score(X_te, y_te):+.4f}")
# Fit a forest first to learn what is achievable, then decide whether the
# boosting tuning effort is worth the difference.
Worked Examples
Bagging divides variance; boosting divides the residual
Bagging: variance. Suppose $n=10$ models each have variance $\sigma^2 = 1$ and are independent. Their average has variance
\text{Var} \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1
Averaging cuts variance tenfold. It does not reduce bias: if every model is biased by $+2$, the average is biased by $+2$ too. That is why bagging suits high-variance learners such as deep trees.
Boosting: bias. Target $y = 10$. Each stage fits the current residual with a learner that captures half of it (learning rate $0.5$), so the prediction $F_k$ after $k$ stages satisfies
The residual halves each stage: $F_k = 10(1-0.5^k)$. Boosting attacks bias step by step, which is why it suits high-bias (weak) learners such as stumps.
Summary. Bagging: parallel, reduces variance, cannot fix bias. Boosting: sequential, reduces bias, can overfit if run too long.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
We need LBLV models; regularization, bagging and
 boosting are the three techniques.

Bagging uses LBHV models — e.g. a fully grown decision tree.
 Boosting uses HBLV models — e.g. a shallow tree with
 max_depth$=1$.

Bagging does parallel learning — all models trained at the same
 time. Boosting does sequential learning — step by step, each
 correcting the previous one.

In bagging the weightage of base learners is the same — every
 model has an equal say. In boosting it is different — a better
 model has a better say, and vice versa.

All of this follows from one fact: bagging attacks variance,
 boosting attacks bias.
Bagging cannot overfit by adding members; boosting can.

Bagging is robust to label noise; boosting — AdaBoost
 especially — is sensitive to it.

Bagging parallelises; boosting cannot. Bagging gives free
 OOB validation; boosting does not.

Boosting usually wins on clean tabular data when tuned; a random
 forest is the better default.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is the fundamental difference between bagging and boosting?

Which error term they attack. Bagging averages independent models to reduce
variance; boosting composes models sequentially, each correcting the last,
to reduce bias. Every other difference — base learner, training order,
weighting, noise robustness — follows from that.
Q. Why does bagging use deep trees and boosting use stumps?

Because they need opposite raw material. Bagging removes variance and cannot touch
bias, so it wants low-bias, high-variance learners. Boosting removes bias, so it
wants high-bias, low-variance ones it can accumulate.

Q. Why do the models get equal weight in bagging but different weights in
boosting?

In bagging every model is an exchangeable draw from the same procedure, so there
is no reason to prefer one. In boosting each model is fitted to a different,
progressively harder problem, and its weight $\alpha_m$ encodes how well it did on
it — a better model earns a bigger say.
Q. Can you overfit by adding more estimators?

Not with bagging — more members only drive $\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$ towards
zero. With boosting, yes: each stage keeps reducing training error, so past some
point it starts fitting noise. Boosting therefore needs n_estimators tuned,
usually with early stopping.
Q. Your labels are about 15% noisy. Which do you use?

Bagging. Boosting up-weights points it gets wrong, and a mislabelled point can
never be got right, so its weight grows exponentially and the ensemble ends up
fitting the errors. Bagging averages the noise away instead.
Q. Which is better?

On clean tabular data a well-tuned gradient-boosting model is usually the most
accurate. But a random forest is the better default: it is far harder to
misconfigure, robust to noise, parallel, and gives an OOB estimate for free. Fit
the forest first, then decide whether the boosting tuning is worth it.
